stem: A stakeholder requests the highest-capability model tier for a task that cross-references eleven internal memos partly contradicting each other, twice a month, ahead of a risk brief the general counsel must sign. Which response fits?

opts.t: Deny the request and assign the smallest/fastest model, since this is a high-volume, latency-gated classification workload.
Push back on the request and ask what specifically about the task requires that level of capability.
Approve the request and select the single most capable frontier model available, regardless of cost.
Approve the higher-capability tier — the memo cross-referencing is a genuine, stated complexity driver, not an unbounded ask for headroom.

whyRight: The memos partly contradicting each other is a genuine, stated complexity driver, not an unbounded ask for headroom — task complexity, not volume, is the binding constraint here, so approving a higher-capability tier, not necessarily the single most capable model, is the right response.

whyWrong.A: The stem states this task runs twice a month and involves cross-referencing memos — that is low-volume synthesis, not the high-volume, latency-gated classification workload this option's reasoning assumes.
whyWrong.B: Pushing back is the right move only when no complexity driver is stated; here the memo cross-referencing already supplies one, so approving the higher tier is appropriate, not premature.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the stated driver calls for the single most capable model regardless of cost; that buys unpriced headroom beyond what the memo-contradiction complexity actually requires.

t1Clause: cross-references eleven internal memos partly contradicting each other

factAnswerRaw: Push back — ask what specifically requires it
stem: A product director, alarmed by a competitor's public AI mishap, insists a customer-support summarizer use the largest model available 'to be safe,' without citing any accuracy or compliance figure it currently misses. What should the lead do?

opts.t: Approve the request — a higher-capability model is warranted whenever a stakeholder raises a safety concern.
Deny the request outright and keep the current model, without asking what specific concern is driving it.
Push back and ask what specific accuracy, latency, or compliance requirement the current model actually fails to meet.
Approve switching to the largest available model without evaluating the cost of running it at the summarizer's request volume.

whyRight: No accuracy, latency, or compliance figure is cited — only a fear following a competitor's incident. Per the guide, headroom bought without a stated requirement is unpriced cost, not safety, so the lead should surface what driver, if any, actually justifies the upgrade.

whyWrong.A: A higher-capability model fits when task complexity is the stated driver; here the trigger is a stakeholder's fear after someone else's incident, not a named requirement.
whyWrong.B: Declining is directionally right, but stopping there skips the actual point of pushing back — surfacing what specific requirement, if any, the current model is failing to meet.
whyWrong.D: This approves the swap without checking what running the largest model would cost at the summarizer's actual request volume — exactly the discriminator the decision is supposed to weigh.

t1Clause: without citing any accuracy or compliance figure it currently misses

stem: A 200-person help-desk deployment needs a formatting rule to hold for the life of the conversation. A team member proposes having each user type the rule into their own first message when a session starts. What should the team do?

opts.t: Move the rule into the system prompt; a first-message rule loses authority once the conversation moves past that turn.
Keep the plan, but also set the same rule as an environment variable at deploy time for redundancy.
Keep the plan, but reword the instruction to be more explicit and specific.
Approve the plan as-is; a rule stated at a session's start already carries authority through the rest of it.

whyRight: The rule sits in the first user message, not the system prompt — the only location with authority across an entire conversation. A first-message rule is not durable; once the conversation moves past that turn, nothing keeps the model honoring it for the rest of the 200-person deployment.

whyWrong.B: Environment variables are infrastructure configuration; they don't reach the model at all, so this doesn't make the rule durable — it just relocates the same non-solution to deploy time.
whyWrong.C: This treats a placement problem as a wording problem — rewording doesn't fix where the rule lives; a first-message rule loses authority once the conversation moves on.
whyWrong.D: This states a rule was said at some point, but doesn't establish where — a first-message rule specifically does not carry authority once the conversation moves past that turn.

t1Clause: have each user type the rule into their own first message

stem: An agent must enforce a hard refusal boundary across every account-closure conversation it handles: never process a closure without a second human's sign-off, escalating automatically otherwise, before a compliance audit next quarter. Select two practices that satisfy this requirement.

opts.t: Let closures proceed normally, but log every one for a reviewer to audit after the fact.
State the sign-off rule once, in the agent's first message of each new conversation.
Write the refusal-and-escalation rule directly into the system prompt as an explicit instruction the agent must follow.
Finalize the boundary's design before deployment, rather than adding it later as a reactive monitoring rule.

whyRight: Both are correct: the boundary must be written into the system prompt to have any authority at all, and it must be designed before deployment — a guardrail is a design decision made at system-prompt time, not a monitoring rule bolted on afterward.

whyWrong.A: The requirement is a hard refusal boundary that blocks unauthorized closures before they happen. Logging and auditing afterward detects misuse instead of preventing it.
whyWrong.B: A rule stated in a conversation's first message is not durable — it loses authority once that conversation ends, and cannot enforce a boundary across every conversation.

t1Clause: across every account-closure conversation it handles
